title: Sémillon
description: Bordeaux's golden grape: the heart of Sauternes and the secret of Hunter Valley's long-lived whites.
L: Sémillon gives medium to full-bodied whites with lemon, lanolin, beeswax, grass and, with age, honey, toast and nuts. Acidity is low to medium, texture waxy and oily. Young, it can seem neutral; its strength is texture and ageing. It's Bordeaux's most planted white grape.

Sémillon's thin, golden skins make it prone to rot, including noble rot, Botrytis cinerea. That's a weakness in wet years but a gift for sweet wine. It's vigorous and productive. In Bordeaux it's often blended with Sauvignon Blanc, which adds acidity and aroma to Sémillon's body.
Thin skins, prone to noble rot
Why is Sémillon so suited to noble rot?
Thin skins let Botrytis cinerea attack easily.

Look for pale to medium lemon colour, a subtle nose of lemon, lanolin and sometimes grass, and a waxy, round palate. In blends with Sauvignon, Sémillon adds weight and texture. Aged Sémillon is unmistakable: toast, honey and lemon curd, even without oak.
Not true. Its thin skins make it prone to rot and noble rot.
Sémillon gives lemon, lanolin and a waxy texture
Thin skins make it prone to noble rot
It's often blended with Sauvignon Blanc

Sémillon is Bordeaux's most planted white grape. It's blended with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle in dry whites, from Entre-Deux-Mers to Pessac-Léognan, and in sweet wines, from Sauternes, Barsac, Loupiac and Cadillac. Bergerac and Monbazillac, nearby, also use it.

Australia is Sémillon's other great home: the Hunter Valley for unoaked, long-lived dry wines; Margaret River for Sémillon Sauvignon Blanc blends; the Barossa for richer, oaked styles. South Africa once had over 90% Sémillon in the 19th century; now old vines remain. Chile and Argentina grow it too.
Match each place to its Sémillon.

Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc complement each other: Sémillon gives body, texture and ageing potential; Sauvignon gives aroma and acidity. In dry Bordeaux, the blend can age for decades. In Sauternes, Sémillon usually makes up about 80%, with Sauvignon adding freshness.
What does Sémillon add to a blend with Sauvignon Blanc?

Australia's Hunter and Margaret River are key homes
With Sauvignon, it balances body and freshness
Explain how noble rot affects Sémillon

In Sauternes and Barsac, the cool Ciron river meets the warmer Garonne, creating autumn mists. Morning humidity lets Botrytis cinerea grow; sunny afternoons stop grey rot. On Sémillon's thin skins, the fungus shrivels berries, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour, and adding honey, apricot and marmalade.

Pickers pass through the vineyard several times, called tries, choosing only botrytised berries. Yields can be tiny, a glass of wine per vine at Château d'Yquem. Wines are fermented and aged in oak for up to three years, reaching about 13 to 14% alcohol and 100 to 150 g/l of sugar.
Put the making of Sauternes in order.
Mist and sun bring noble rot
Noble rot first, then careful selection, then slow fermentation and ageing.

Sauternes is one of the longest-lived wines. Over decades, it darkens from gold to amber, developing crème brûlée, saffron, dried apricot and marmalade. Good vintages last 50 years or more. Château d'Yquem, the only Premier Cru Supérieur of 1855, is the most famous.
What is a trie in Sauternes?
A pass through the vineyard to pick botrytised berries
Several tries pick only the berries that are ready.
The Ciron's mists bring noble rot to Sémillon
Pickers make several tries; yields are tiny
Sauternes ages for decades, darkening to amber
A dry wine that ages like magic

The Hunter Valley, north of Sydney, is hot and humid, with rain often at harvest. Growers pick Sémillon early, at around 10 to 11% alcohol, before the rain and rot. The wines are fermented in steel, without oak or malolactic, and bottled early. Young, they're lean, lemony and grassy, with high acidity.

With 5 to 10 years in bottle, often under screw cap, Hunter Sémillon transforms: it develops toast, honey, lanolin, lemon curd and nutty notes, as if it had been oaked. It isn't: these flavours come from bottle ageing. The best can age 20 years or more.
Hunter Valley Sémillon's toasty notes come from oak ageing.
Not true. It's usually unoaked; toast and honey develop with bottle age.
If you find a 10-year-old Hunter Valley Sémillon, open it next to a young one. The difference shows how far bottle ageing can take a simple, unoaked wine.
Why is Hunter Sémillon picked so early?
To avoid harvest rain and rot, and keep acidity
Early picking keeps freshness and avoids the region's harvest rains.
Hunter Sémillon is picked early, at 10 to 11%, unoaked
With age it gains toast and honey, without oak

Young Hunter Sémillon suits oysters, sashimi and light seafood. Aged Hunter and dry Bordeaux blends suit roast chicken, crab, lobster, and creamy fish dishes. Margaret River Sémillon Sauvignon suits salads, goat's cheese and summer food.

Sauternes suits foie gras, a Bordeaux classic, and blue cheese, especially Roquefort, whose salt balances the sweetness. It also suits fruit tarts, crème brûlée and spicy Asian dishes. Serve at 8 to 10 degrees. Avoid desserts much sweeter than the wine.
Match each Sémillon to a pairing.
Serve dry Sémillon at 8 to 11 degrees. Young Hunter is crisp and lean; wait 10 years for its magic. Dry white Bordeaux ages 10 to 20 years. Sauternes ages 20 to 50 years or more.
Roquefort and Sauternes is a classic pairing.
Yes. Salt balances sugar, and the wine's acidity cuts the cheese's fat.
Young dry Sémillon suits seafood; aged suits chicken and crab
